extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in algebraic geometry / commutative algebra (learning criteria and properties of flatness)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and collects the many equivalent criteria, tests, and properties for flatness of modules and morphisms (Tor-characterizations, ideal-theoretic/equational criteria, local criteria over special rings, behavior under base change, geometric consequences such as openness, going-down, fiber-dimension formulas, and generic freeness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tor characterization of flatness
rubrics_metrics.description: M is A-flat if and only if Tor^A_1(M, N) = 0 for all A-modules N. (Exercise 23.1.C referenced.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard homological criterion: compute Tor by resolving one entry and checking vanishing of Tor_1. Use this to deduce many consequences; later sections re-use properties of Tor. (See Exercises 24.3.A–24.3.C for computations and consequences.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal-theoretic criterion for flatness (Theorem 24.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The A-module M is flat if and only if Tor^A_1(M, A/I) = 0 for every ideal I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently (see Remarks), the natural map I ⊗_A M → IM is injective for every ideal I. It suffices to check finitely generated ideals (see 24.4.3). This formulation leads to concrete checks on closed subschemes and fibers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equational criterion for flatness (24.4.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-module M is flat iff for every relation ∑_i a_i m_i = 0 (with a_i ∈ A, m_i ∈ M) there exist m'_j ∈ M and a_{ij} ∈ A with m_i = ∑_j a_{ij} m'_j and ∑_i a_i a_{ij} = 0 for all j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translation: every A-linear relation among elements of M 'comes from' relations in A. This is the concrete 'equational' way to check flatness and can be used to construct witnesses in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of finitely generated ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: In Theorem 24.4.1 it suffices to check Tor^A_1(M, A/I) = 0 only for finitely generated ideals I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the argument: a counterexample for a non-finitely-generated ideal yields one for a finitely-generated ideal. This makes the ideal-theoretic test practical in many settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatness over a PID: flat = torsion-free (24.4.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Over a principal ideal domain, an A-module is flat if and only if it is torsion-free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful concrete classification: check torsion-free condition rather than Tor computations. See Exercise 24.4.B for proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatness over a DVR (24.4.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer t, then an A-module M is flat iff t is not a zerodivisor on M (i.e., (M : t) = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields a direct geometric interpretation for maps to regular curves: flatness ⇔ no uniformizer is a zerodivisor on the fiber/module.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatness over the dual numbers (24.4.D)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A = k[t]/(t^2), M is flat iff the multiplication-by-t map M/tM → tM is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concrete finite-ideal classification is important in deformation theory; k[t]/(t^2) has only three ideals, enabling an elementary check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat = free = projective for finitely presented modules over local rings (24.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose (A,m) is a local ring and M is a finitely presented A-module. Then M is flat iff M is free iff M is projective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a key local criterion: finitely presented + flat implies freeness (use Nakayama and finite presentation). Warning: over local rings a module can be flat without being free if not finitely presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finitely presented sheaf flat ⇔ locally free (24.4.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A finitely presented sheaf F on X is flat over X iff it is locally free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check at stalks. Geometric corollary of 24.4.5; useful to interpret flatness of coherent sheaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pullback preserves powers of ideal sheaves under flat morphism (24.2.O)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is flat and I is an ideal sheaf cutting out Z ⊂ Y, then (π^* I)^n = π^*(I^n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Products/powers of quasicoherent ideal sheaves commute with flat pullback; see Exercise 24.2.O and its hint to use properties of quasicoherent sheaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pullback of quasicoherent ideal sheaves for flat closed subschemes (24.3.2, 24.3.H)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a fiber product diagram and V flat over Z, the two possible pullbacks of the ideal sheaf of X agree: α^* I_{V/X} ≅ I_{Y×_Z V / W}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark 14.5.10 warned these need not agree in general; flatness of the relevant map (here V→Z) ensures equality. Hint: use Exercise 24.3.D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blowing up commutes with flat base change (24.2.P)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y ⊂ X is a closed embedding and π: X' → X is flat, then Bl_Z Y ×_Y X' ≅ Bl_{Z×_Y X'} X'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove via universal property (Exercise 24.2.N(a)) or via Proj construction of the blowup and the behaviour of graded sheaves under flat pullback (see 24.2.O). Provide a counterexample showing blowup need not commute with arbitrary base change (24.2.P(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tor base-change under flat extension (24.3.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If B is A-flat then there is an isomorphism B ⊗_A Tor^A_i(M, N) ≅ Tor^B_i(M⊗_A B, N⊗_A B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the FHHF Theorem (finitely presented, homological base-change facts) to derive this; useful for transporting Tor computations along flat maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactness preserved by tensoring with flat modules (24.3.C–24.3.F)
rubrics_metrics.description: If 0 → N' → N → N'' → 0 is exact and N'' is flat (e.g., free), then 0 → M⊗_A N' → M⊗_A N → M⊗_A N'' → 0 is exact for any A-module M. More generally, tensoring an exact sequence with a flat module preserves exactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both a definition-level property and a practical tool (see Exercise 24.3.D for the sheaf version under pullback). Use the long exact Tor-sequence for proofs of related closure properties (24.3.E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful flatness: definition and equivalent tests (24.5.1–24.5.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: A B-module M is faithfully flat if for any complex of B-modules N'→N→N'' the complex is exact iff after tensoring with M it is exact. Equivalently: M is flat and M⊗_B N = 0 implies N = 0; equivalently for all primes p⊂B, M⊗_B κ(p) ≠ 0; equivalently for all maximal ideals m, M⊗_B κ(m) ≠ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For morphisms of schemes, π: Spec A → Spec B is faithfully flat iff π is flat and surjective. Use these tests to recognize faithful flatness in practice (Exercise 24.5.B, 24.5.C, 24.5.D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Going-Down theorem for flat morphisms (24.5.E)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is flat over B and q'⊂q are primes of B and p' is a prime of A with image q', then there exists a prime p of A with p'⊂p and image q (i.e., you can lift chains of primes downward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by localizing and using faithful flatness (Exercise 24.5.D(b)). This gives geometric consequences: flat morphisms satisfy a going-down property for specialization of points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat morphisms are open in reasonable situations (24.5.G)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is locally of finite type and flat, with Y (hence X) locally Noetherian, then π is an open map.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Chevalley's theorem to show image is constructible, Going-Down to show closed under generization, and then standard criteria to conclude openness. Counterexamples show the finite-type / Noetherian hypotheses are necessary in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensions of fibers formula for flat maps (Proposition 24.5.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is flat (locally Noetherian), p ∈ X, q = π(p), then codim_X p = codim_Y q + codim_{π^{-1}(q)} p. Informally: fiber dimension = dim X − dim Y (locally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One inequality is general (Exercise 12.4.A); the other uses Going-Down for flat morphisms. Consequence: for irreducible varieties π flat ⇒ all fibers have pure dimension dim X − dim Y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat of relative dimension n (definition and base-change stability) (24.5.9, 24.5.K)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π: X → Y is 'flat of relative dimension n' if π is flat, locally of finite type, and all fibers have pure dimension n. This property is preserved under arbitrary base change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'locally of finite type' hypothesis ensures reasonability and base-change behaviour; see Remarks 24.5.11 for motivation and counterexamples without this hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic freeness (Grothendieck's Generic Freeness Lemma 24.5.13) and generic flatness (24.5.R)
rubrics_metrics.description: If B is a Noetherian integral domain and A a finitely generated B-algebra, then A (and finitely generated A-modules) satisfy the property that there exists nonzero f ∈ B with localization making modules free over B_f. Consequently, for a finite-type morphism π: X → Y with Y integral Noetherian and a coherent sheaf F on X, there exists a dense open U ⊂ Y over which F is flat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved via a sequence of exercises (24.5.L–24.5.Q). The geometric corollary (generic flatness) is central: flatness holds over a dense open in many finite-type situations; apply to O_X to get generic flatness of the morphism itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat limits: closure of generic fiber is flat (24.4.13, 24.4.K, 24.4.L)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a DVR with generic point η and X is a locally Noetherian A-scheme, and Y is a closed subscheme of X|_η, then the scheme-theoretic closure Y' of Y in X is flat over A. Moreover, such a flat extension Y' with Y'|_η = Y is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes taking 'flat limits' in one-parameter families; Exercise 24.4.L gives an explicit example and 24.4.K shows uniqueness. Use criterion 24.4.J (flatness over regular curves) in proofs.
